title: Paradox Interactive 的《Afterworld》想用诱人的 RPG 钩子吸引新玩家进入大战略游戏
content:
Afterworld boasts grand strategy with tasty RPG hooks
Design
Interviews
Paradox Interactive's Afterworld wants to entice new players to grand strategy with tasty RPG hooks
Game director Dan Lind explains the appeal of strategy in grand strategy games, and how to invite new players into a sprawling game.
Alessandro Fillari
,
Contributor
September 1, 2026
7 Min Read
Via Paradox
One of the appeals of the grand strategy genre is the awesome sense of scale: you're building a sprawling civilization from the ground up, making key decisions on allocating resources and making plays to expand your influence. For those who can immerse themselves in games such as Sid Meier's Civilization, Hearts of Iron, and Crusader Kings, it can offer unparalleled moments of storytelling and agency—but for less experienced players, just getting started can be daunting.
That's where the upcoming grand strategy game
Afterworld
from Paradox Interactive is looking to shake things up. While still very much about the experience of cultivating a civilization in the making,
Afterworld
brings sprawling 4x4 and grand strategy gameplay to a post-apocalyptic setting, where all factions—known as tribes—will have to learn how to survive and thrive within a world slowly rebuilding itself. It's a game that puts discovery and cultural development front and center, alongside mutants, cyborg billionaires, and rival tribes with a taste for human flesh.
Related:
Warlock's magic system was built on game-bending player choices
After getting a first look at
Afterworld
, game director Dan Lind of Paradox Development Studio explained that this post-apocalyptic sandbox is the team’s effort to open up the grand strategy genre to new players. One secret to
Afterworld
’s recipe: a keen focus on role-playing elements is key to pushing the genre even further.
"We have always been very focused on the audience that we have with our games, and I hope all of them will like this too, but since we've grown as a company, we want to broaden the audience more as well," said game director Dan Lind. "When it comes to games like this, it's always about that 4X experience of starting small and expanding as a necessity, but making that easy for all players to get into can be a challenge. I'm not sure how I would do this with Hearts of Iron, honestly, because it's like you're starting in the middle of history. But that's why I like this version of a post-apocalyptic setting [with
Afterworld
], it's like we're restarting history and putting all players in that space forging that path into the unknown."
The game's setting is North America, centuries after total ruin. The remaining clusters of survivors are isolated from one another, with some cultures living in secluded bunkers, surviving on the surface in makeshift towns, or living in protected cities in service to former rich men (turned cyborg deities), the player's chosen tribe will steadily branch out into the larger world. On this new path of rediscovery, players will establish and expand territory, interact with other surviving groups, and build up a new civilization of their own making—all while trying to co-exist or face off against others who may have conflicting interests.
Related:
How you (yes, you) can benefit from 1-on-1 synchronous playtesting
Paradox Development Studio has been at the forefront of the grand strategy genre for a long time, with recent hits like
Stellaris
,
Hearts of Iron IV
, and
Crusader Kings III
. With
Crusader Kings III
in particular, the team not only innovated on the complex diplomacy and kingdom-building gameplay for a Middle Ages setting, but it also further emphasized that one of the great strengths of the genre is storytelling. Players weave fascinating yearns as they shape their own nations and characters, and deal with the causality of their choices.
For
Afterworld
, the developers were keen to focus on player choice within a post-apocalyptic setting. It certainly taps into the complex expansion systems and branching threads of choices found in other games in the genre.
Afterworld
puts more of a focus on getting your tribe to a place where they'll be able not just to survive and build a network of communities, but also evolve as a culture. Of course, what that looks like in-game is entirely up to the player.
Related:
How Forbidden Solitaire brought solitaire games to the forefront
"That's something I'm betting on a lot, it's why I decided to make the tribe origins in
Afterworld
a bit like building your backstory of sorts," said the game director. "Instead of going the
Stellaris
route where it's a lot of settings to tune, we're gonna try to ease you into playing a role-playing game with your tribe, essentially. I think for people who are not used to how a grand strategy game works, it can be quite hard to understand that you can do anything and to find out what your own goal is. With
Afterworld
, it's gonna make you adapt and stay in the moment. I think at some point you'll realize you've actually set goals for yourself and you're able to do stuff. So I'm hoping we'll be able to attract people who are invested in [the] story and won't have to think too much about number crunching."
Playing the early stages of
Afterworld
as the Shelterborn tribe felt akin to a strategic roadtrip. One tribe we got to see in action was the Shelterborn, a community of survivors who lived in vaults and were isolated from the changed surface world. By stepping out of their decaying shelter—which explodes after a few phases pass—this particular faction has to figure out how to navigate an unfamiliar world. This starts with building safe havens and securing resources, but eventually expands to communicating with other roaming tribes, and even the nearby warlords who may demand your loyalty.

Afterworld
's most intriguing concepts: the tribe's core ideas. Presented in
